bib.title: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models: Principles, Taxonomy, Challenges, and Open Questions
bib.venue: ACM Transactions on Information Systems, Vol. 1, No. 1, Article 1 (January 2024)

question: What are the types, causes, detection methods, benchmarks and mitigations of hallucination in LLMs, and where do retrieval-augmented systems still fail?
contributions: A redefined taxonomy of LLM hallucination: factuality vs faithfulness (Sec 2.3)
Analysis of causes across data, training and inference (Sec 3)
Overview of detection methods and benchmarks (Sec 4)
Analysis of hallucination in RAG: retrieval failure and generation bottleneck (Sec 6)
Future directions: vision-language models, knowledge boundaries (Sec 7)

results.claim: LLM hallucination is split into factuality hallucination and faithfulness hallucination; faithfulness has three subtypes (instruction, context, logical inconsistency).
results.setup: Survey text; no experiments run by the survey authors
results.quote: We categorize hallucination into two primary types: factuality hallucination and faithfulness hallucination.

results.claim: Faithfulness hallucination is divergence from user input or lack of self-consistency; factuality is discrepancy from verifiable real-world facts.
results.setup: Survey text; no experiments run by the survey authors
results.quote: Factuality hallucination emphasizes the discrepancy between generated content and verifiable real-world facts, typically manifesting as factual inconsistencies.

results.claim: Context inconsistency is the grounding-relevant faithfulness subtype: output unfaithful to the provided/retrieved context (Table 1 uses a retrieved Nile passage).
results.setup: Survey text; no experiments run by the survey authors
results.quote: Context inconsistency points to instances where the LLM’s output is unfaithful with the user’s provided contextual information.

results.claim: Prior NLG taxonomy kept as background: intrinsic = contradicts source; extrinsic = cannot be verified from source or external knowledge.
results.setup: Survey text; no experiments run by the survey authors
results.quote: Specifically, intrinsic hallucinations pertain to the model outputs that directly conflict with the provided source context.

results.claim: Factual fabrication (unverifiable against real-world knowledge) is split into unverifiability and overclaim hallucination; factual contradiction into entity-error and relation-error.
results.setup: Survey text; no experiments run by the survey authors
results.quote: Factual Fabrication refers to instances where the LLM’s output contains facts that are unverifiable against established real-world knowledge.

results.claim: Detection is split by hallucination type: factuality detection vs faithfulness detection (faithfulness judged against provided context).
results.setup: Survey text; no experiments run by the survey authors
results.quote: (2) faithfulness hallucination detection, which focuses on evaluating the faithfulness of model’s outputs to the contextual information provided.

limits: The survey runs no experiments; every number is a benchmark size or a figure described from cited work.
Table 4 gives FELM 3,948 data size but Sec 4.2.2 says 817 samples; unreconciled.
Table 1 logical-inconsistency example prints x=3 in the dialog but the text (Sec 2.3.2) says final answer x=4.
Authors concede RAG is hit by irrelevant retrieval, shallow retriever-generator interaction, and that self-correction (post-editing) may be unreliable (Sec 5.1.3, 5.3.1).
Authors concede lie-detector/probing methods for LLM internal beliefs are not yet reliable (Sec 7.2).
Literature cutoff is 2024; later RAG-grounding evaluators and benchmarks are not covered.
Does not give a single recommended grounding metric or compare detectors quantitatively.
practices: Detect factuality hallucination by extracting atomic facts and verifying each against trusted sources (Sec 4.1.1).
Use uncertainty estimation (token probability, entropy, sample consistency) when no retrieval source is available or only API access exists (Sec 4.1.1).
Assess faithfulness to provided context with fact-overlap, NLI classifier, QA-based, uncertainty-based or LLM-judge metrics (Sec 4.1.2).
Prefer benchmarks matching the task: QA benchmarks for factuality, summarization/document benchmarks for faithfulness; Table 4 marks which attribute each tests.
Query rewriting and decomposition for ambiguous/complex queries; adaptive retrieval instead of blind retrieval (Sec 6.1.1).
Use source attribution and faithful decoding in RAG (Sec 6.2.2).

terms.definition: the discrepancy between generated content and verifiable real-world facts, typically manifesting as factual inconsistencies
the divergence of generated content from user input or the lack of self-consistency within the generated content
the LLM’s outputs that deviate from a user’s directive
instances where the LLM’s output is unfaithful with the user’s provided contextual information
internal logical contradictions in outputs, often in reasoning tasks, between steps or between steps and final answer
model outputs that directly conflict with the provided source context
outputs that cannot be verified using the provided source context or external knowledge bases
output contains facts that can be grounded in real-world information but present contradictions (entity-error, relation-error)
output contains facts that are unverifiable against established real-world knowledge (unverifiability, overclaim)
